items.label: f01-durable-before-visible
items.front: Order of operations for a crash-safe local JSON commit?
items.back: Write a temp file, fsync, close, renameSync over the data file, and only then publish the new state in memory. A lock file opened with 'wx' is the writer lease (EEXIST becomes 503, never waited on or stolen).

items.label: f03-uncertain-vs-conflict
items.front: How does an uncertain response differ from a 409 conflict, and how does the UI handle it?
items.back: A conflict means the server refused; an uncertain response (network failure) means it may already have committed. The UI marks the write uncertain and blocks further saves until the user reviews the latest state, because without receipts a retried POST could create a second record.

items.label: f02-global-key-oracle
items.front: Flag keys are unique across all projects and the 409 says 'Flag key "X" already exists'. Risk and fix?
items.back: It is an oracle revealing other projects' keys to anyone who can create flags. Decide key scope explicitly: per-project keys (audit every key-only lookup) or global keys with a generic message.

items.label: f04-authorize-first
items.front: Rule for ordering validation that reads stored data against authorization?
items.back: Authorize first. Validation messages derived from a stored record describe it to whoever asked; run requireProjectWrite before validateStrategySettings (and validateVariant), keeping only the low-risk 404 on random ids ahead of the 403.

items.prompt: A constraint is rewritten as plan not_in [free]. A context arrives with no plan field. What does the constraint evaluate to, and why?

choices.text: false: a missing or non-scalar context value never matches, even through not_in or inversion, so missing data cannot switch a flag on
true only when inversion is enabled
true, because an absent plan is not 'free'
It throws, and the whole evaluation fails closed with a 500

choices: false: a missing or non-scalar context value never matches, even through not_in or inversion, so missing data cannot switch a flag on
true only when inversion is enabled
true, because an absent plan is not 'free'
It throws, and the whole evaluation fails closed with a 500

items.explanation: evaluation.js returns false when the raw value is not scalar, before any operator logic; removing that line would let every plan-less context through to the rollout check.

items.prompt: Why would answering evaluate requests with 304 Not Modified keyed on the snapshot ETag be a bug?

choices.text: Because ETags change on every request, so a 304 would never actually be returned to any client
Because the snapshot cache evicts entries too quickly to serve 304s reliably under load
It is not a bug; flag decisions are the same for every user of a snapshot
The ETag names the configuration, not the caller; one snapshot gives different users different answers

choices: Because ETags change on every request, so a 304 would never actually be returned to any client
Because the snapshot cache evicts entries too quickly to serve 304s reliably under load
It is not a bug; flag decisions are the same for every user of a snapshot
The ETag names the configuration, not the caller; one snapshot gives different users different answers

items.explanation: With checkout_redesign at 25% rollout, one ETag maps to four different results across contexts; the cache key says nothing about who asked.

items.prompt: Why does #commit publish the new state in memory only after renameSync succeeds?

choices.text: To keep the in-memory cache smaller during the write
If memory were published first, readers could see a change that a later disk failure rolled back: durability must come before visibility
Because renameSync is asynchronous and must be awaited first
Because the lease file is deleted by renameSync

choices: To keep the in-memory cache smaller during the write
If memory were published first, readers could see a change that a later disk failure rolled back: durability must come before visibility
Because renameSync is asynchronous and must be awaited first
Because the lease file is deleted by renameSync

items.explanation: The file is written, fsynced and renamed into place, then #accept publishes the exact bytes; the guide calls durability and visibility separate events.

items.prompt: bucketValue maps users to 1..100 and a rollout matches when bucket <= rollout. Why is the range 1..100 rather than 0..99?

choices.text: So rollout 0 enables nobody and rollout 100 everybody
Because JavaScript's % operator cannot return 0
So that a missing userId can be assigned bucket 0
Because SHA-256 digests never produce a zero prefix

choices: So rollout 0 enables nobody and rollout 100 everybody
Because JavaScript's % operator cannot return 0
So that a missing userId can be assigned bucket 0
Because SHA-256 digests never produce a zero prefix

items.explanation: (numeric % range) + 1 shifts the range; a boundary test built on bucketValue itself catches the off-by-one that 200 random users rarely hit.

items.prompt: Two sibling variants each have weight 60. Why can no single-field validator reject that, and what inconsistency does the codebase have here?

choices.text: Weights are validated only in the browser, so the server accepts any sum
Each 60 is valid on its own; only the sum breaks the 'variants sum to 100' rule, and that rule answers 422 in the contract but 400 (bad sum) or 409 (duplicate name) in the service
The rule is enforced only at evaluation time, which silently normalizes the weights
A weight of 60 is out of range, and both layers consistently return 422

choices: Weights are validated only in the browser, so the server accepts any sum
Each 60 is valid on its own; only the sum breaks the 'variants sum to 100' rule, and that rule answers 422 in the contract but 400 (bad sum) or 409 (duplicate name) in the service
The rule is enforced only at evaluation time, which silently normalizes the weights
A weight of 60 is out of range, and both layers consistently return 422

items.explanation: Cross-field invariants need a set-level check; the review (R3) recommends standardizing semantic failures on 422 so clients can tell a conflict from a malformed request.

items.prompt: A project_member of the Checkout project holds a token with the write scope and tries to edit a flag in a different project. What happens?

choices.text: 401: the token is rejected because it was issued while the user was working in Checkout
200: a write-scoped token can edit any project's flags, because scope is the only check on writes
403: the write scope is not enough without a membership row for that project
404: flags in other projects are invisible to every non-admin

choices: 401: the token is rejected because it was issued while the user was working in Checkout
200: a write-scoped token can edit any project's flags, because scope is the only check on writes
403: the write scope is not enough without a membership row for that project
404: flags in other projects are invisible to every non-admin

items.explanation: Effective permission is the intersection of token scope, instance role and per-project membership; only instance_admin skips the membership check.

items.prompt: An editor loaded revision 8 and saves with If-Match: "8", but another user committed revision 9 in between. Why are the service's permission checks still safe even though they are check-then-act?

choices.text: Checks use the request's frozen snapshot, and the commit is refused (409) if version or digest changed
Because the service re-runs every permission and confirmation check after the write succeeds and reverts on failure
They are not safe; the second write silently overwrites revision 9
Because the writer lease blocks all other reads while any editor has a form open in the browser

choices: Checks use the request's frozen snapshot, and the commit is refused (409) if version or digest changed
Because the service re-runs every permission and confirmation check after the write succeeds and reverts on failure
They are not safe; the second write silently overwrites revision 9
Because the writer lease blocks all other reads while any editor has a form open in the browser

items.explanation: Under #withLease the store compares meta.version and the digest with what the request expected; any mismatch throws 'State changed; reload and review before saving'.

items.prompt: A flag is { description: 'Old text', stale: true }. A PATCH sends { description: '' }. What is stored afterwards?

choices.text: description 'Old text', because an empty string is falsy and ignored
description '' and stale false, because omitted booleans default to false
The PATCH is rejected with 422 because description cannot be empty
description '' and stale still true

choices: description 'Old text', because an empty string is falsy and ignored
description '' and stale false, because omitted booleans default to false
The PATCH is rejected with 422 because description cannot be empty
description '' and stale still true

items.explanation: updateFlag uses !== undefined for description and the booleans, so '' and false are applied while omitted fields are untouched; only name and type use truthiness, which is safe because the contract refuses an empty name.

items.prompt: Someone hand-edits data/state.json without changing meta.version. Which part of the commit condition catches it?

choices.text: The writer lease, because the editor holds the lock file
The digest comparison, so the next mutation gets 409
The version comparison, because any write to the file bumps meta.version
Nothing; the next mutation overwrites the hand edit

choices: The writer lease, because the editor holds the lock file
The digest comparison, so the next mutation gets 409
The version comparison, because any write to the file bumps meta.version
Nothing; the next mutation overwrites the hand edit

items.explanation: If the version were the only check, a stale draft would be accepted and silently overwrite the edit; test/storage.test.js:124 covers this.

items.prompt: A token is revoked while a client still holds the actor object built from it earlier. What does its next service call return, and why?

choices.text: 401: the wrapper re-reads the token on every call and requires it unrevoked
Success until the actor object's cached expiry passes, after which the next call returns 401
Success, because the actor object was already authenticated when the session started
403, because revoked tokens keep read access only

choices: 401: the wrapper re-reads the token on every call and requires it unrevoked

items.explanation: The per-request re-read costs one scan but makes revocation effective mid-session; the review lists it as deliberate, not a finding.

items.prompt: Why does variant selection hash 'variant:<flagKey>:<userId>' instead of reusing the rollout bucket input?

choices.text: Because the rollout bucket is stored per user and variants are not
So variant choice is independent of rollout position
Because the rollout hash uses MD5, which is too short for variants
So that a user's variant changes on every request for fairness

choices: Because the rollout bucket is stored per user and variants are not
So variant choice is independent of rollout position
Because the rollout hash uses MD5, which is too short for variants
So that a user's variant changes on every request for fairness

items.explanation: Rollout bucketing hashes '<groupId>:<userId>'; reusing it would correlate low buckets with particular variants. Both are deterministic, so nothing is stored.
